questions.question: Explain Andrew’s experiments on isotherms of a real gas and discuss their / significance.
questions.solution_html:
• Andrew’s studied the behavior of carbon dioxide by plotting pressure–volume curves at
  • constant temperatures (isotherms), particularly at 13.1°C, 21.5°C and 31.1°C, to understand
  • liquefaction of real gases. A fixed amount of CO₂ was enclosed in a strong tube with a piston, and
  • pressure was applied while maintaining constant temperature, recording the corresponding
  • volume changes.
  • At 13.1°C, which is well below the critical temperature (31.1°C) of carbon dioxide, Andrew’s
  • isotherm shows a clear and detailed pattern of liquefaction with three distinct regions. Initially
  • in the gaseous region (A–B), CO₂ behaves nearly like an ideal gas, where an increase in pressure
  • intermolecular forces are negligible. As compression continues, the curve reaches a
  • horizontal portion (B–C), which represents the liquefaction region. In this region, the
  • pressure remains constant while the volume decreases significantly, showing that gas
  • is being converted into liquid. At point B, liquefaction begins, and between B and C
  • liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. At point C, the entire gas is converted into
  • liquid. This constant pressure is the vapour pressure of CO₂ at 13.1°C. Beyond this, in
  • the liquid region (C–D), further increase in pressure causes only a very small decrease
  • in volume, producing a steep curve because liquids are almost incompressible. Thus
  • the isotherm at 13.1°C clearly demonstrates the process of liquefaction of a real gas, showing
  • distinct gaseous, transition, and liquid regions, which is characteristic of temperatures below the
  • critical temperature.
  • At 21.5°C (still below critical temperature but closer to Tc), similar behavior is observed, but the
  • length of the horizontal region decreases, indicating that liquefaction occurs over a smaller volume
  • range. This shows that as temperature increases, liquefaction becomes more difficult.
  • At 31.1°C (critical temperature of CO ), the horizontal portion disappears and is replaced by a point
  • of inflection, called the critical point. At this temperature, the distinction between liquid and gas
  • vanishes, and CO₂ exists as a critical fluid. Beyond this temperature, no amount of pressure can
  • liquefy the gas.
  • (Experiment with suitable explanation -(7 marks), diagram (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option (c) of carbon dioxide, Andrew’s
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discuss the Lowry-Bronsted theory and the Lewis theory of acids and bases. / Explain a simple eutectic system using lead-silver as an example. Apply phase
questions.solution_html:
• The Lowry–Brønsted theory defines an acid as a proton (H⁺) donor and a base as a proton (H⁺)
  • acceptorAccording to this theory, every acid–base reaction involves the transfer of a proton from
  • the acid to the base. For example, in the reaction HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl donates a proton
  • and acts as an acid, while water accepts the proton and acts as a base. This theory also
  • introduces the concept of conjugate acid–base pairs, where an acid forms its conjugate base after
  • donating a proton, and a base forms its conjugate acid after accepting a proton (e.g., HCl/Cl⁻ and
  • H₂O/H₃O⁺). However, the Lowry–Brønsted concept is limited to reactions involving proton
  • transfer and cannot explain acid–base reactions where no proton is involved. (Definition – (2 marks)
  • Explanation with example – (3 marks))
  • The Lewis theory provides a more general definition, where an acid is a species that accepts an
  • electron pair and a base is a species that donates an electron pair. (Definition – (2 marks)) For
  • example, in the reaction BF₃ + NH₃ → BF₃←NH₃, boron trifluoride (BF₃) acts as a Lewis acid by
  • accepting an electron pair from ammonia (NH₃), which acts as a Lewis base, forming a coordinate
  • covalent bond. The Lewis theory is more comprehensive because it includes reactions that do not
  • involve protons and explains a wider range of chemical behavior, including complex formation and
  • catalytic reactions. (Definition – (2 marks), Explanation with example – (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: catalytic reactions. (Definition – , Explanation with example – )

questions.question: / rule.
questions.solution_html:
• The lead–silver (Pb–Ag) system is a simple eutectic system consisting of two components that
  • are completely miscible in the liquid state but almost immiscible in the solid state. The
  • diagram plots temperature on the y-axis and composition on the x-axis (from 100% Pb to 100%
  • Ag).At the top region A–B, the system exists entirely in the liquid state. The two curves
  • A–O and B–O are called liquidus curves, which represent the temperatures at which
  • solidification begins. As a molten mixture cools, the behavior depends on its
  • composition.For a lead-rich alloy (left side), cooling from point A follows the liquidus curve
  • A–O. At point y, solid lead (Pb) starts to crystallize, and the system enters a two-phase
  • region (liquid + solid Pb). As cooling continues, more Pb separates out and the liquid
  • becomes richer in silver until it reaches point O, the eutectic point.For a silver-rich alloy
  • (right side), cooling follows curve B–O. At point R, solid silver (Ag) begins to separate, and
  • the system enters the region (liquid + solid Ag). With further cooling, more silver
  • crystallizes, and the liquid composition shifts toward the eutectic composition until point
  • O is reached.The point O (2.6% Ag, 303°C) is the eutectic point, where the liquid transforms
  • simultaneously into a fine mixture of solid Pb and solid Ag. This occurs at a constant
  • temperature, and below this temperature, the system consists entirely of solid phases.The
  • horizontal line C–D (303°C) represents the eutectic temperature, below which only solid
  • phases exist. The regions below this line are
  •  Left side: Solid Pb + eutectic mixture
  •  Right side: Solid Ag + eutectic mixture
  • Thus, the diagram clearly shows three important regions
questions.final_answer: Option (c) is the eutectic point, where the liquid transforms

questions.question: Evaluate a Minimum Boiling Azeotrope and a Maximum Boiling Azeotrope by / relating them to their respective types of Raoult's Law deviations.
questions.solution_html:
• respective types of Raoult's Law deviation.
  • A Type II non-ideal solution shows Large positive deviation from Raoult’s law, meaning the total
  • vapour pressure of the solution is greater than predicted for an ideal solution. This occurs because
  • the intermolecular forces between unlike molecules (A–B) are weaker than those between like
  • molecules (A–A and B–B), so molecules escape more easily
  • into the vapour phase.In the vapour pressure–composition
  • curve, the experimental curve lies above the Raoult’s law
  • straight line, indicating higher vapour pressure at all
  • compositions.In the temperature–composition (boiling point)
  • curve, the solution shows a minimum boiling point, because
  • higher vapour pressure leads to lower boiling
  • temperature.Examples: Ethanol–water, acetone–carbon
  • disulfide.A Type III non-ideal solution shows large negative
  • deviation from Raoult’s law, where the observed vapour
  • pressure is lower than predicted. This is due to stronger intermolecular forces between unlike molecules
  • (A–B) compared to like molecules, reducing the tendency of molecules to escape into vapour
  • phase. In the vapour pressure–composition curve, the actual curve lies below the Raoult’s law line
  • indicating reduced vapour pressure. In the temperature–composition curve, this leads to a maximum
  • boiling point, since lower vapour pressure requires higher temperature for boiling. Example
  • Acetone–chloroform system.
  • Minimum Boiling Azeotrope and a Maximum Boiling Azeotrope is out of syllabus, so Reasonable attempt
  • of type II and type III non ideal solutions with suitable explanation and curves can be give full credit.
questions.final_answer: Option (b) are weaker than those between like

questions.question: Explain Andrew’s experiments on isotherms of a real gas and discuss their / significance.
questions.solution_html:
• Andrew’s studied the behavior of carbon dioxide by plotting pressure–volume curves at
  • constant temperatures (isotherms), particularly at 13.1°C, 21.5°C and 31.1°C, to understand
  • liquefaction of real gases. A fixed amount of CO₂ was enclosed in a strong tube with a piston, and
  • pressure was applied while maintaining constant temperature, recording the corresponding
  • volume changes.
  • At 13.1°C, which is well below the critical temperature (31.1°C) of carbon dioxide, Andrew’s
  • isotherm shows a clear and detailed pattern of liquefaction with three distinct regions. Initially
  • in the gaseous region (A–B), CO₂ behaves nearly like an ideal gas, where an increase in pressure
  • intermolecular forces are negligible. As compression continues, the curve reaches a
  • horizontal portion (B–C), which represents the liquefaction region. In this region, the
  • pressure remains constant while the volume decreases significantly, showing that gas
  • is being converted into liquid. At point B, liquefaction begins, and between B and C
  • liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium. At point C, the entire gas is converted into
  • liquid. This constant pressure is the vapour pressure of CO₂ at 13.1°C. Beyond this, in
  • the liquid region (C–D), further increase in pressure causes only a very small decrease
  • in volume, producing a steep curve because liquids are almost incompressible. Thus
  • the isotherm at 13.1°C clearly demonstrates the process of liquefaction of a real gas, showing
  • distinct gaseous, transition, and liquid regions, which is characteristic of temperatures below the
  • critical temperature.
  • At 21.5°C (still below critical temperature but closer to Tc), similar behavior is observed, but the
  • length of the horizontal region decreases, indicating that liquefaction occurs over a smaller volume
  • range. This shows that as temperature increases, liquefaction becomes more difficult.
  • At 31.1°C (critical temperature of CO ), the horizontal portion disappears and is replaced by a point
  • of inflection, called the critical point. At this temperature, the distinction between liquid and gas
  • vanishes, and CO₂ exists as a critical fluid. Beyond this temperature, no amount of pressure can
  • liquefy the gas.
  • (Experiment with suitable explanation -(7 marks), diagram (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: Option (c) of carbon dioxide, Andrew’s

questions.question: Discuss the Lowry-Bronsted theory and the Lewis theory of acids and bases. / Explain a simple eutectic system using lead-silver as an example. Apply phase
questions.solution_html:
• The Lowry–Brønsted theory defines an acid as a proton (H⁺) donor and a base as a proton (H⁺)
  • acceptorAccording to this theory, every acid–base reaction involves the transfer of a proton from
  • the acid to the base. For example, in the reaction HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, HCl donates a proton
  • and acts as an acid, while water accepts the proton and acts as a base. This theory also
  • introduces the concept of conjugate acid–base pairs, where an acid forms its conjugate base after
  • donating a proton, and a base forms its conjugate acid after accepting a proton (e.g., HCl/Cl⁻ and
  • H₂O/H₃O⁺). However, the Lowry–Brønsted concept is limited to reactions involving proton
  • transfer and cannot explain acid–base reactions where no proton is involved. (Definition – (2 marks)
  • Explanation with example – (3 marks))
  • The Lewis theory provides a more general definition, where an acid is a species that accepts an
  • electron pair and a base is a species that donates an electron pair. (Definition – (2 marks)) For
  • example, in the reaction BF₃ + NH₃ → BF₃←NH₃, boron trifluoride (BF₃) acts as a Lewis acid by
  • accepting an electron pair from ammonia (NH₃), which acts as a Lewis base, forming a coordinate
  • covalent bond. The Lewis theory is more comprehensive because it includes reactions that do not
  • involve protons and explains a wider range of chemical behavior, including complex formation and
  • catalytic reactions. (Definition – (2 marks), Explanation with example – (3 marks))
questions.final_answer: catalytic reactions. (Definition – , Explanation with example – )

• The lead–silver (Pb–Ag) system is a simple eutectic system consisting of two components that
  • are completely miscible in the liquid state but almost immiscible in the solid state. The
  • diagram plots temperature on the y-axis and composition on the x-axis (from 100% Pb to 100%
  • Ag).At the top region A–B, the system exists entirely in the liquid state. The two curves
  • A–O and B–O are called liquidus curves, which represent the temperatures at which
  • solidification begins. As a molten mixture cools, the behavior depends on its
  • composition.For a lead-rich alloy (left side), cooling from point A follows the liquidus curve
  • A–O. At point y, solid lead (Pb) starts to crystallize, and the system enters a two-phase
  • region (liquid + solid Pb). As cooling continues, more Pb separates out and the liquid
  • becomes richer in silver until it reaches point O, the eutectic point.For a silver-rich alloy
  • (right side), cooling follows curve B–O. At point R, solid silver (Ag) begins to separate, and
  • the system enters the region (liquid + solid Ag). With further cooling, more silver
  • crystallizes, and the liquid composition shifts toward the eutectic composition until point
  • O is reached.The point O (2.6% Ag, 303°C) is the eutectic point, where the liquid transforms
  • simultaneously into a fine mixture of solid Pb and solid Ag. This occurs at a constant
  • temperature, and below this temperature, the system consists entirely of solid phases.The
  • horizontal line C–D (303°C) represents the eutectic temperature, below which only solid
  • phases exist. The regions below this line are
  •  Left side: Solid Pb + eutectic mixture
  •  Right side: Solid Ag + eutectic mixture
  • Thus, the diagram clearly shows three important regions

questions.question: Evaluate a Minimum Boiling Azeotrope and a Maximum Boiling Azeotrope by / relating them to their respective types of Raoult's Law deviations.
questions.solution_html:
• respective types of Raoult's Law deviation.
  • A Type II non-ideal solution shows Large positive deviation from Raoult’s law, meaning the total
  • vapour pressure of the solution is greater than predicted for an ideal solution. This occurs because
  • the intermolecular forces between unlike molecules (A–B) are weaker than those between like
  • molecules (A–A and B–B), so molecules escape more easily
  • into the vapour phase.In the vapour pressure–composition
  • curve, the experimental curve lies above the Raoult’s law
  • straight line, indicating higher vapour pressure at all
  • compositions.In the temperature–composition (boiling point)
  • curve, the solution shows a minimum boiling point, because
  • higher vapour pressure leads to lower boiling
  • temperature.Examples: Ethanol–water, acetone–carbon
  • disulfide.A Type III non-ideal solution shows large negative
  • deviation from Raoult’s law, where the observed vapour
  • pressure is lower than predicted. This is due to stronger intermolecular forces between unlike molecules
  • (A–B) compared to like molecules, reducing the tendency of molecules to escape into vapour
  • phase. In the vapour pressure–composition curve, the actual curve lies below the Raoult’s law line
  • indicating reduced vapour pressure. In the temperature–composition curve, this leads to a maximum
  • boiling point, since lower vapour pressure requires higher temperature for boiling. Example
  • Acetone–chloroform system.

  • of type II and type III non ideal solutions with suitable explanation and curves can be give full credit.
